newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK to enjoy more monetary autonomy after handover.
newsitem.headline: HK to enjoy more monetary autonomy after handover.

text.p: Hong Kong will enjoy a higher degree of monetary autonomy after it returns to Beijing in July as a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China , the territory's top monetary official said.

"In fact, the degree of monetary autonomy the SAR will enjoy will be higher than what Hong Kong at present enjoys as a British colony," Joseph Yam said in an article published on Monday in the South China Morning Post .
Yam heads the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the territory's defacto central bank. The colony reverts to China at midnight on June 30, after more than 150 years of British rule.

Current rules say the governor may not assent to "any Bill affecting the Currency of the Colony or relating to the issue of Bank notes", or "any Bill establishing any Banking Association, or amending or altering the constitution, powers, or privileges of any Banking Association" without London's prior approval.

"Under the Basic Law, there is only the corresponding general requirement that laws enacted by the SAR legislature must be reported to the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress for the record," he said.
The Basic Law, the constitution for post-colonial Hong Kong, also specifies that "the reporting for record shall not affect the entry into force of such laws", Yam said.
The higher degree of autonomy the SAR will enjoy is also evident in recent changes to monetary legislation, Yam said.
"Amendments have been introduced in the past few years, after consultation with the Chinese side, to ensure the relevant Hong Kong laws are consistent with the Basic Law," he said.

"One significant amendment common in this exercise is the removal of the need to refer matters to the Secretary of State for approval, which, if not removed, would mean the need to refer matters to the State Council of the People's Republic of China after July," he said.
The State Council is China's cabinet.

"After these amendments, our autonomy in monetary affairs, to the extent they do not involve matters of defence and/or foreign affairs, will be equivalent to that enjoyed by any economy with its own currency," he said.
The territory will not change its banking supervisory policy as a result of the handover, Yam said.
"It is important we maintain a level playing field for all banking institutions wanting to establish themselves and operate in Hong Kong," he said.
"Our banking policy will not be tilted in favour of banking institutions from any jurisdiction, including those from China," he added.
